summary.overview: Enzymes are biological catalysts, almost all of them proteins. They speed up reactions under mild conditions, with high specificity, and their activity can be regulated. Many need a cofactor or coenzyme, and each enzyme is named and numbered by the reaction it catalyses.

sections.heading: General properties
points: Almost all enzymes are proteins; a few catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) also exist.
Catalytic activity depends on the native protein conformation; denaturation destroys it.
Advantages over inorganic catalysts: greater specificity (no side products), mild conditions (pH ≈ 7, 37 °C), much higher rates, and the ability to be regulated.
The reaction takes place in the active site, a pocket that binds the substrate.

sections.heading: Cofactors and coenzymes
points: Cofactor: one or more inorganic ions, such as Fe²⁺, Mg²⁺, Mn²⁺ or Zn²⁺.
Coenzyme: a complex organic or metallo-organic molecule that carries functional groups temporarily. Most are derived from vitamins.
Prosthetic group: a coenzyme or cofactor bound very tightly, often covalently, so it is a permanent part of the enzyme.
Holoenzyme = apoenzyme (the protein part) + its cofactor or coenzyme.

sections.heading: Classification
points: Enzymes are grouped into six classes by reaction: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases.
Each enzyme has a four-part EC number. Hexokinase is 2.7.1.1: transferase → phosphotransferase → OH group as acceptor → D-glucose as acceptor.
Most names end in -ase; some keep old names such as pepsin and lysozyme.

sections.heading: Specificity
points: Specificity comes from the precise three-dimensional fit between substrate and active site.
Papain cleaves almost any peptide bond, which is why it is used to tenderise meat.
Trypsin cleaves only on the carboxyl side of Lys and Arg; thrombin cleaves only specific Arg–Gly bonds.

sections.heading: Isozymes
points: Isozymes catalyse the same reaction but differ in amino acid sequence, because they are encoded by different genes.
They differ in kinetics or regulation and can be separated by electrophoresis.
Lactate dehydrogenase is a tetramer of H and M chains. M4 works best in anaerobic skeletal muscle; H4 works best in aerobic heart muscle.
Tissue-specific isozymes in serum help diagnose organ damage.

sections.heading: How catalysis works
points: Enzymes lower the activation energy (ΔG‡). They do not change ΔG or K′eq.
Binding energy holds reactants close together and in the right orientation, paying the entropy cost during binding.
Active sites are complementary to the transition state, so they bind it more tightly than the substrate (Pauling).

keyTerms.definition: Pocket on the enzyme where substrate binds and the reaction occurs.
Inorganic ion required for activity, e.g. Zn²⁺ or Mg²⁺.
Organic molecule that carries groups temporarily; usually vitamin-derived.
Cofactor or coenzyme bound very tightly or covalently to the enzyme.
Complete, active enzyme with its cofactor or coenzyme bound.
The protein part of an enzyme without its cofactor.
Four-part code: class, subclass, sub-subclass and serial number.
Different protein, from a different gene, that catalyses the same reaction.

examTips: Coenzymes are organic (often vitamin-derived); cofactors in the narrow sense are metal ions. Read the wording carefully.
The first EC digit gives the class: 1 oxidoreductase, 2 transferase, 3 hydrolase, 4 lyase, 5 isomerase, 6 ligase.
Isozymes catalyse the SAME reaction but are products of DIFFERENT genes.
An enzyme speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so K′eq is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which statement about biological catalysts is correct?

options.text: Almost all are proteins, but some catalytic RNAs (ribozymes) also exist
options.why: Ribozymes show that RNA can catalyse reactions, which suggests RNA acted as a biocatalyst early in evolution.

options.text: Every enzyme is a protein, without exception, including the ribosome's catalytic site
options.why: Catalytic RNAs such as the ribosome's peptidyl transferase are exceptions.

options.text: Enzymes are used up as the reaction proceeds, so cells must keep making new copies
options.why: Like all catalysts, enzymes are regenerated unchanged at the end of each catalytic cycle.

options.text: Enzymes keep their full activity after their structure is denatured by heat
options.why: Catalytic activity depends on the native conformation; denaturation destroys it.

questions.stem: Chorismate could break down by several chemical routes, yet in the cell chorismate mutase converts it almost entirely to prephenate. Which advantage of biological catalysts does this illustrate?

options.text: Greater reaction specificity, which avoids side products
options.why: The enzyme makes one pathway much faster than the others, so the desired product dominates.

options.text: Enzymes shift the equilibrium of the reaction towards prephenate
options.why: Enzymes never change K′eq; they only change rates.

options.text: Enzymes work only at high temperature, where side reactions stop
options.why: Enzymes work under mild cellular conditions, around 37 °C and pH 7.

options.text: Enzymes make the overall ΔG of the reaction more negative
options.why: ΔG depends only on the initial and final states, not on the catalyst.

questions.stem: Hexokinase has the EC number 2.7.1.1. What does the first digit, 2, tell you?

options.text: It is a transferase: it moves a group (here a phosphoryl) from one molecule to another
options.why: Class 2 = transferases; the 7 then specifies phosphotransferases.

options.text: It is an oxidoreductase: it transfers electrons from glucose to an acceptor such as NAD⁺
options.why: Oxidoreductases are class 1.

options.text: It is a hydrolase: it uses water to split the phosphoanhydride bond between ATP's phosphates
options.why: Hydrolases are class 3.

options.text: Its substrate is glucose: the first digit identifies the sugar that the enzyme acts on
options.why: The substrate (D-glucose as acceptor) is given by the last digit, not the first.

questions.stem: Trypsin breaks peptide bonds by adding water across them. To which enzyme class does it belong?

options.text: Hydrolases (class 3)
options.why: Hydrolases cleave bonds using water, e.g. peptidases, lipases and phosphatases.

options.text: Oxidoreductases (class 1)
options.why: Oxidoreductases transfer electrons, e.g. dehydrogenases.

options.text: Transferases (class 2)
options.why: Transferases move groups between molecules, e.g. kinases.

options.text: Lyases (class 4)
options.why: Lyases break bonds without water or oxidation, often forming double bonds (e.g. aldolase).

options.text: Ligases (class 6)
options.why: Ligases join molecules using energy from ATP.

questions.stem: Lactate dehydrogenase catalyses pyruvate + NADH + H⁺ ⇌ lactate + NAD⁺. To which class does it belong?

options.text: Oxidoreductases
options.why: Electrons (as a hydride) pass from NADH to pyruvate: a redox reaction, class 1.

options.text: Isomerases (class 5)
options.why: Isomerases rearrange atoms within one molecule; here NADH is oxidised and pyruvate reduced.

options.text: Ligases (class 6)
options.why: No new bond is formed using ATP.

options.text: Lyases (class 4)
options.why: No group is removed to form a double bond.

questions.stem: What is the catalytically active complex of an apoenzyme with its cofactor or coenzyme called?

options.text: Holoenzyme
options.why: Holoenzyme = apoenzyme (protein) + cofactor or coenzyme: the complete, active enzyme.

options.text: Prosthetic group
options.why: This is the tightly bound cofactor itself, not the whole complex.

options.text: Zymogen
options.why: A zymogen is an inactive precursor activated by proteolysis.

options.text: Isozyme
options.why: Isozymes are different proteins that catalyse the same reaction.

questions.stem: Which of these is best described as a prosthetic group?

options.text: Biotin covalently attached to a lysine residue of pyruvate carboxylase
options.why: A prosthetic group is bound so tightly (here covalently) that it is a permanent part of the enzyme.

options.text: NAD⁺, which binds a dehydrogenase, accepts electrons and then diffuses away
options.why: NAD⁺ binds only temporarily and moves between enzymes, so it acts as a co-substrate.

options.text: Mg²⁺ that binds loosely from solution to activate a kinase
options.why: A loosely bound metal makes the enzyme metal-activated; it is not a prosthetic group.

options.text: ATP consumed as a substrate by hexokinase
options.why: ATP is a substrate that is converted to ADP.

questions.stem: Cats fed mainly raw fish that contains thiaminase can develop neurological signs. Why are key metabolic enzymes affected?

options.text: Thiamine is the precursor of thiamine pyrophosphate, a coenzyme needed by pyruvate dehydrogenase
options.why: Most coenzymes come from vitamins. Without thiamine, TPP-dependent enzymes can't work, and neurons, which rely on glucose oxidation, suffer first.

options.text: Thiaminase directly hydrolyses the peptide bonds of enzymes in the brain, destroying their structure
options.why: Thiaminase destroys the vitamin, not proteins.

options.text: Thiamine is an inorganic cofactor that stabilises the folded structure of many metabolic enzymes
options.why: Thiamine is an organic vitamin; inorganic cofactors are metal ions.

options.text: Thiamine deficiency raises the activation energy of most enzymes in the body
options.why: Only enzymes that need TPP are affected.

questions.stem: Trypsin acts on the peptide Ala–Lys–Gly–Phe–Arg–Ser. Which peptide bonds does it cleave?

options.text: Lys–Gly and Arg–Ser
options.why: Trypsin cleaves on the carboxyl side of the basic residues Lys and Arg.

options.text: Phe–Arg only
options.why: Cleavage after aromatic residues like Phe is typical of chymotrypsin, not trypsin.

options.text: Every peptide bond in the chain
options.why: That broad pattern describes papain, not the highly specific trypsin.

options.text: Ala–Lys and Phe–Arg
options.why: These bonds are on the amino side of Lys and Arg; trypsin cuts on the carboxyl side.

questions.stem: Why is papain, from papaya, used commercially to tenderise meat?

options.text: It cleaves almost any peptide bond, whatever the neighbouring side chains
options.why: Its low specificity lets it break down many different muscle and connective-tissue proteins.

options.text: It cleaves only the Arg–Gly bonds in fibrinogen, which softens the meat's clots
options.why: That highly specific activity describes thrombin.

options.text: It forms new disulfide bonds in collagen, which soften the meat's connective tissue
options.why: Papain hydrolyses peptide bonds; it does not create cross-links.

options.text: It works only after the meat is fully cooked, when the collagen has turned to gelatin
options.why: Cooking denatures and inactivates enzymes; papain works before cooking.

questions.stem: Which statement about isozymes is correct?

options.text: They catalyse the same reaction but differ in sequence, kinetics or regulation, from different genes
options.why: Isozymes are distinct proteins for the same reaction, often separable by electrophoresis.

options.text: They catalyse different reactions using the same active site, depending on which substrate is present
options.why: Isozymes catalyse the SAME reaction.

options.text: They are identical proteins, encoded by one gene, that are found in different organelles of the cell
options.why: Isozymes differ in amino acid sequence.

options.text: They are inactive precursors that are activated by proteolysis when the cell needs the enzyme
options.why: That describes zymogens.

questions.stem: Why is the M4 isozyme of lactate dehydrogenase well suited to hard-working skeletal muscle?

options.text: It works well in anaerobic conditions, reducing pyruvate to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis
options.why: M4 suits the anaerobic environment of intense muscle work; H4 suits the aerobic heart.

options.text: It is encoded by the same gene as the H4 isozyme, but it is folded differently in skeletal muscle
options.why: H and M chains come from different genes; that is what makes them isozymes.

options.text: It is a monomer rather than a tetramer, so it diffuses faster through the crowded muscle cytosol
options.why: Every functional LDH is a tetramer.

options.text: Skeletal muscle has no other way to make ATP, because its fibres contain no mitochondria at all
options.why: Muscle also uses oxidative phosphorylation when O2 is available.

questions.stem: A horse shows muscle stiffness and reluctance to move after exercise ('tying-up'). Which serum enzyme activity is most useful for confirming skeletal muscle damage?

options.text: Creatine kinase (CK)
options.why: CK, mainly the muscle MM isoform, leaks from damaged muscle fibres and rises sharply within hours.

options.text: Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
options.why: ALP mainly reflects bone, liver or bile-duct changes.

options.text: Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT)
options.why: GGT is a marker of liver and bile-duct disease.

options.text: Lipase
options.why: Lipase is used to assess the pancreas.

questions.stem: How does an enzyme use substrate-binding energy to speed up a reaction between two molecules?

options.text: It pays the entropy cost of bringing the reactants together in the correct orientation
options.why: Holding reactants rigidly in the ES complex means the conversion to the transition state no longer loses much entropy.

options.text: It heats the active site above the surrounding temperature, so the reactants collide faster
options.why: Enzymes work at the temperature of their surroundings.

options.text: It makes the overall ΔG of the reaction more negative, so the products form more readily
options.why: ΔG is fixed by the reactants and products; only ΔG‡ is lowered.

options.text: It stores the binding energy as ATP and spends it later to drive the reaction forward
options.why: Binding energy is used directly in the catalytic step, not stored.

questions.stem: An enzyme speeds up the conversion of A to B a million-fold. What happens to the reverse reaction (B → A) and to K′eq?

options.text: The reverse reaction is also a million times faster, and K′eq is unchanged
options.why: Lowering ΔG‡ speeds both directions equally, so their ratio, K′eq, stays the same.

options.text: The reverse reaction is unchanged, so K′eq rises a million-fold
options.why: An enzyme cannot speed up only one direction; that would violate thermodynamics.

options.text: The reverse reaction slows down, pushing the reaction to completion
options.why: Enzymes never slow the reverse reaction or change the final equilibrium.

options.text: K′eq falls, because the enzyme binds B and removes it from the reaction
options.why: Binding products does not change the equilibrium constant.

questions.stem: Why would an enzyme whose active site was perfectly complementary to the substrate, rather than to the transition state, be a poor catalyst?

options.text: Tight substrate binding stabilises ES, deepening an energy well and raising the barrier to the transition state
options.why: Catalysis needs the strongest interactions to form in the transition state, which lowers ΔG‡ (Pauling).

options.text: The substrate could no longer enter the active site, because the site would already be filled by water
options.why: A complementary site would bind the substrate very well; the problem lies in what happens next.

options.text: The enzyme would change K′eq in favour of the substrate
options.why: Enzymes cannot change K′eq whatever they bind.

options.text: The enzyme would become irreversibly inhibited by its own product
options.why: Product binding is not what is described here.

flashcards.back: Almost all. Ribozymes are catalytic RNA molecules.
Cofactor: an inorganic ion (Fe²⁺, Mg²⁺, Mn²⁺, Zn²⁺). Coenzyme: an organic or metallo-organic molecule that carries groups temporarily; most come from vitamins.
A cofactor or coenzyme bound very tightly, often covalently, so it is a permanent part of the enzyme.
Holoenzyme: the active enzyme with its cofactor bound. Apoenzyme: the protein part alone.

flashcards.front: The six main enzyme classes, in EC order?
flashcards.back: 1 Oxidoreductases, 2 Transferases, 3 Hydrolases, 4 Lyases, 5 Isomerases, 6 Ligases. (A 7th class, translocases, was added in 2018.)
2 transferase · 7 phosphotransferase · 1 OH group as acceptor · 1 D-glucose as acceptor.

flashcards.front: Papain vs trypsin vs thrombin specificity?
flashcards.back: Papain: almost any peptide bond. Trypsin: carboxyl side of Lys/Arg. Thrombin: specific Arg–Gly bonds only.
Different proteins (different genes) that catalyse the same reaction, with different kinetics or regulation. Separable by electrophoresis, e.g. LDH H4 vs M4.
M4: anaerobic, hard-working skeletal muscle. H4: aerobic heart muscle.

flashcards.front: Why do enzymes bind the transition state best?
flashcards.back: Extra interactions with the transition state lower ΔG‡ (Pauling, 1946). Transition-state analogues are therefore potent inhibitors.
